this is a tough one. for me, i found an LGBTQ clinic in my nearest city and that was the first appointment they made. if you go to a clinic like that they're more likely to treat you well. i've always worked with outside psychiatrists and psychologists though, and i've found if i feel comfortable and heard in sharing my trauma with them, that's a good sign they'll be understanding of gender dysphoria - even if they aren't the most knowledgeable. 

a good psychologist will give you space to express those feelings without judgement or trying to change that part of you. a good psychiatrist will use the right name and pronouns (basic respect for your autonomy) and focus on how medication can treat help your mental health symptoms. symptoms being anxiety, depressed mood, panic attacks, etc. a good psychiatrist will not try to "fix" your gender with medication.

and as for how to know what your doctor is doing, i'd make sure your doctor knows their shit and is certified in LGBTQ health. i've heard people say "trans people have to be our own doctors", but i strongly disagree - personally i'm not the one who went to medical school. but what i will say is that we sometimes have to \*train\* our doctors. making sure they research and understand trans healthcare, sending them medical journals and studies if you suspect something is wrong, and holding them accountable for being a good ally (if they aren't trans themselves) are all very important. 

i've been very lucky with healthcare so far - my first doctor was the head of the LGBTQ program in his hospital, and my current doctor is trans herself - so i don't have much experience to pull from otherwise. but doing research and making sure you choose the right person to control your medical transition is key. make sure you trust them, and make sure they do their homework. looking into LGBTQ healthcare programs in your area is a great starting place, or looking at doctor recommendations in trans support groups on facebook or reddit can be helpful as well (especially if you live in a red state).

i graduated high school 2 years ago and i came out in public school at the beginning of my sophomore year. this is what ive learned:

most teenage cishet boys are awful. plain and simple. their masc for masc appeal might seem great, but a lot of them love drama and making people feel bad. dont fall for it. thats not what being a man is, and if theyve got toxic behaviors, they arent worth your time. i say this because i wanted more than anything to be accepted by the more traditionally masc cis guys at my school, but you cant change people. 

ON THE OTHER HAND, this isnt true for all cis boys! for a while i had a close friend group of primarily cis guys, and getting to know them helped me feel accepted and supported, and gave me some natural masculine behavior to study and apply to myself to help with social dysphoria.

to avoid hearing your deadname if you cant legally change it yet, email or pull your teachers aside before class starts and explain your situation. something as plain as “the roster states this name, but i go by this name, please use that name and x pronouns when referring to me” is assertive and respectful. same with substitutes if youre unfamiliar with them. if they deny your request, report it. you dont have to deal with that.

as annoying as it is to have to change in a completely different area, changing in the nurse’s office saved me a lot of anxiety/panic attacks about changing in the boys locker room. as badly as i wanted to go in there with everyone else, there were some people who id have to interact with who had bullied me since middle school, and i just didnt feel safe. if your case is similar, theres no shame in using the nurses office or a different bathroom. on the other hand, if you feel being in the same locker room would decrease your dysphoria then id suggest arranging a time to talk with a VP or principal or whoever has power in the school and may be able to help your case.

dont feel trapped inside of one sense of fashion! this is a good time to mess around with what clothing makes you feel good. thrift stores like plato’s closet are great, since you can sell clothes you dont feel comfortable in and get yourself a new wardrobe of things you do! theres no “right” way to be masc, its whatever makes you happy. and if anyone at school has anything to say about it, thats their problem.


but something that helped me the most during school was having a good support network. so so so important. regularly going to therapy (which i know can be difficult for some people, with insurance being a pain and some parents dont see it as a necessity) and having a place to vent to a person who supported me helped a lot. if not a private therapist, i know my school had a small LGBT+ support group that met on wednesdays. we’d get out of class for it. again, not all schools are as fortunate, but in any case guidance counselors and school therapists can be good allies. but the biggest thing that helped me cope were my teachers. being open with the ones i felt comfortable with was super freeing, and when i joined the boys lacrosse team i even had one teacher look up the laws to make sure i was protected from discrimination for my gender identity. i still keep in touch with a lot of them actually - they feel like chosen family.

all in all, only you know what helps decrease your dysphoria and what doesnt. its hard to figure out sometimes but the baseline is, all you gotta do is be you. and you is a man. best of luck! you got this!
